directAnswer: St. Peter was Simon, a Galilean fisherman from Bethsaida whom Jesus called as an apostle and renamed Cephas, or Peter, meaning “rock.” The Gospels show him as the leader and spokesman of the Twelve, and the Catholic Church honors him as the first bishop of Rome and the first pope. Ancient tradition holds that he was martyred in Rome under Emperor Nero and buried on the Vatican Hill.

paras: Peter was born Simon, son of Jonah (or John), and the Gospel of John names Bethsaida on the Sea of Galilee as his hometown. He later lived in Capernaum, where he worked as a fisherman with his brother Andrew, in partnership with James and John, the sons of Zebedee. The Gospels mention his mother-in-law, whom Jesus healed, so we know he was married.

According to John’s Gospel, Andrew had followed John the Baptist and brought his brother to Jesus, who looked at him and gave him the new name Cephas, an Aramaic word that, like the Greek Petros, means rock. The Synoptic Gospels describe Jesus calling Simon from his boats with the promise that he would become a fisher of men. From that point Peter appears first in every list of the apostles.

sections.h2: The Keys of the Kingdom at Caesarea Philippi
paras: The scene that grounds Catholic teaching on the papacy takes place near Caesarea Philippi. When Jesus asked the disciples who they said he was, Simon answered that he was the Christ, the Son of the living God. In Matthew 16:18–19 Jesus responds that Simon is Peter, the rock on which he will build his Church, and promises him the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power to bind and loose.

The Gospels do not hide Peter’s weakness. He rebuked Jesus for predicting the Passion, sank when he tried to walk on the water, and three times denied knowing Jesus on the night of the arrest. Yet Luke records that Jesus prayed for Peter’s faith so that he could strengthen his brothers, and John 21 shows the risen Lord asking Peter three times whether he loves him and charging him to feed his lambs and tend his sheep. Catholics read these passages together as the foundation of Peter’s pastoral office.

sections.h2: Leader of the Apostolic Church in Acts
paras: The Acts of the Apostles presents Peter as the head of the young community in Jerusalem. He leads the choice of Matthias to replace Judas, preaches the first public sermon on Pentecost, heals a lame man at the Temple gate, and speaks for the apostles before the Sanhedrin. His baptism of the Roman centurion Cornelius and his household marks the opening of the Church to Gentiles.

At the Council of Jerusalem in Acts 15, Peter argues that Gentile converts should not be burdened with the full Mosaic law, a position the assembly adopts. Paul’s Letter to the Galatians describes meeting Peter in Jerusalem and later confronting him at Antioch over table fellowship with Gentiles, a candid glimpse of how the apostles worked through hard questions. Two New Testament letters bear Peter’s name; the first is addressed to Christians scattered across Asia Minor and sends greetings from “Babylon,” widely understood as a name for Rome.

sections.h2: Martyrdom in Rome and the Tomb Beneath the Basilica
paras: Scripture does not narrate Peter’s death, but very early writers connect him with Rome. Clement of Rome, writing near the end of the first century, speaks of Peter’s suffering and witness, and Ignatius of Antioch and Irenaeus of Lyons treat Peter and Paul as the apostles of the Roman Church. Tradition places his martyrdom in the persecution under Nero; the date c. 67 used on this page follows one ancient reckoning, while others prefer 64. Origen, as reported by Eusebius, records the tradition that Peter asked to be crucified head downward.

Christians honored his grave on the Vatican Hill from an early date, and Emperor Constantine built the first St. Peter’s Basilica over it in the fourth century. Excavations beneath the present basilica, begun in 1939, uncovered a second-century monument at the site, and in 1968 Pope Paul VI announced that bones found there had been identified in a way the Church found convincing. The Church celebrates Peter with Paul on June 29 and keeps the Chair of St. Peter on February 22.

keyFacts: Born Simon in Bethsaida, Galilee; worked as a fisherman at Capernaum with his brother Andrew
Renamed Cephas (Peter, “rock”) by Jesus; received the keys of the kingdom (Matthew 16:18–19)
Preached at Pentecost and spoke at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 2 and 15)
Two New Testament letters, 1 and 2 Peter, bear his name
Martyred in Rome under Nero by ancient tradition; buried on the Vatican Hill
Feast of Sts. Peter and Paul: June 29; Chair of St. Peter: February 22

faqs.question: Why do Catholics consider St. Peter the first pope?
faqs.answer: Catholics point to Jesus naming Simon the rock on which he would build his Church and giving him the keys of the kingdom (Matthew 16:18–19), to the charge to feed his sheep (John 21), and to Peter’s leadership in Acts. Early writers such as Irenaeus traced the bishops of Rome back to Peter and Paul, and the Church sees each pope as Peter’s successor in that office.

faqs.question: Was St. Peter really crucified upside down?
faqs.answer: The tradition is ancient but not found in Scripture. Eusebius reports that Origen said Peter was crucified head downward at his own request. Historians accept that Peter died a martyr in Rome under Nero; the specific detail rests on this early tradition rather than on an eyewitness account.

faqs.question: Is St. Peter actually buried under St. Peter’s Basilica?
faqs.answer: Excavations under the basilica found a second-century shrine marking the place Christians venerated as his tomb, and in 1968 Pope Paul VI announced that bones recovered there had been identified to the Church’s satisfaction. The identification is a matter of careful archaeological judgment rather than absolute proof, but the site’s veneration goes back to the second century.

directAnswer: St. Linus was the second bishop of Rome, the first successor of St. Peter in the earliest lists of Roman bishops. St. Irenaeus wrote that the apostles entrusted the leadership of the Roman Church to Linus, and he is often identified with the Linus who sends greetings in 2 Timothy 4:21. Almost nothing else about his life is known with certainty.

sections.h2: The Linus of Second Timothy and Irenaeus’s List
paras: Around the year 180, St. Irenaeus of Lyons compiled a list of Roman bishops to show that the Church’s teaching came down unbroken from the apostles. He wrote that after founding the Church in Rome, Peter and Paul committed the office of bishop to Linus, and he added that this was the Linus Paul mentions in the Letter to Timothy. That verse, 2 Timothy 4:21, includes Linus among Christians in Rome sending greetings.

Later writers, including Eusebius and Jerome, repeat Irenaeus’s order. A few early sources give a different sequence after Peter, but the place of Linus at the head of the succession is the oldest and best-attested tradition.

The Liber Pontificalis, a collection of papal biographies compiled centuries later, says Linus was an Italian from Tuscia, the region of Etruria, and names his father as Herculanus. It also credits him with requiring women to cover their heads in church, a rule that likely reflects 1 Corinthians 11 more than any decree of his own. Historians treat these details cautiously.

Later tradition honors him as a martyr and says he was buried near Peter on the Vatican Hill, but no early source describes his death. His name is still spoken in the Roman Canon of the Mass, where he heads the list of popes after the apostles, and his feast is kept on September 23.

keyFacts: Second bishop of Rome and first successor of St. Peter in Irenaeus’s list (c. 180)
Probably the Linus greeted in 2 Timothy 4:21
Liber Pontificalis names Tuscia as his homeland and Herculanus as his father
Named in the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I)
Feast day: September 23

faqs.question: Is Pope St. Linus mentioned in the Bible?
faqs.answer: Probably. Paul’s Second Letter to Timothy (4:21) sends greetings from a Roman Christian named Linus, and St. Irenaeus identified him with the second bishop of Rome. The identification is ancient and widely accepted, though Scripture itself says nothing about his later role.

faqs.question: Was St. Linus a martyr?
faqs.answer: The Church has long honored him as a martyr, but no early account of his death survives. The tradition of his martyrdom and burial near St. Peter comes from later sources, so it cannot be confirmed historically.

directAnswer: St. Cletus, also called Anacletus, was the third bishop of Rome, following Linus and preceding Clement in the earliest succession lists. Tradition calls him the first Greek pope, born in Athens. Beyond his place in the list and his commemoration in the Mass, little is known of his life.

paras: Irenaeus of Lyons gives the third bishop of Rome the Greek name Anencletus, meaning blameless or irreproachable. In Latin usage the name was shortened to Cletus, and for a time the two forms caused confusion: the Liber Pontificalis and some later catalogs listed Cletus and Anacletus as two different popes, placing them on either side of Clement. Modern scholarship and the Church’s official lists recognize them as one man.

The Liber Pontificalis describes him as a native of Athens, which is the basis for calling him the first Greek pope. Since Greek was the main language of the Roman Christian community in the first century, a Greek-speaking leader would not have been unusual.

Later tradition credits Cletus with ordaining priests in Rome and with building a memorial at St. Peter’s grave, and it honors him as a martyr, but none of these claims can be traced to first-century evidence. The reign dates given here are approximate, as they are for all the earliest popes.
His name endures in the Roman Canon of the Mass, where he is listed between Linus and Clement. His feast has traditionally been kept on April 26.

keyFacts: Third bishop of Rome, between Linus and Clement in Irenaeus’s list
Greek name Anencletus means blameless; Cletus is the shortened Latin form
Once mistakenly counted as two popes, Cletus and Anacletus
Tradition places his birth in Athens, making him the first Greek pope
Named in the Roman Canon; traditional feast day April 26

faqs.question: Are Pope Cletus and Pope Anacletus the same person?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both names refer to the third bishop of Rome. Some medieval catalogs, including the Liber Pontificalis, treated them as two popes, but historians and the Church now recognize a single pope known by both names.

faqs.question: Why is St. Cletus called the first Greek pope?
faqs.answer: The Liber Pontificalis says he was born in Athens. Because that source is late and not always reliable, the claim reflects tradition rather than documented fact, but his Greek name fits the largely Greek-speaking Roman Church of his day.

directAnswer: St. Clement I was the fourth bishop of Rome and the author, by ancient testimony, of the Letter to the Corinthians known as First Clement, one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament. He is counted among the Apostolic Fathers, and Tertullian said he was ordained by St. Peter. A later legend holds that he was exiled to the Crimea and martyred by being thrown into the sea with an anchor.

sections.h2: A Bishop Who Knew the Apostles
paras: Irenaeus of Lyons places Clement third after Peter and says he had seen the blessed apostles and conversed with them, so that their preaching still echoed in his ears. Tertullian, writing around 200, reports that the Roman Church claimed Clement had been ordained by Peter himself. Origen and Eusebius suggested that he was the Clement Paul names as a fellow worker in Philippians 4:3, though that identification is uncertain.

Nothing reliable survives about his family or early life. A body of later fiction, the Clementine Recognitions and Homilies, makes him a noble Roman who traveled with Peter, but scholars regard these works as third- and fourth-century romances, not history.

sections.h2: First Clement and the Crisis at Corinth
paras: Clement’s lasting importance comes from a letter the Church of Rome sent to the Church of Corinth, usually dated to the mid-90s. Some younger members at Corinth had removed their presbyters from office, and the Roman Church wrote at length to urge repentance, humility, and the restoration of the rightful leaders. The letter does not name its author, but Dionysius of Corinth, around 170, said his church still read aloud the letter written through Clement, and later writers agree.

The letter argues that the apostles appointed bishops and deacons and made provision for others to succeed them, so legitimately appointed ministers should not be thrown out. This makes First Clement an early witness to apostolic succession and to Rome’s concern for another church’s peace, though historians debate how far it reflects papal authority in the later sense. It also contains one of the earliest references to the martyrdom of Peter and Paul.

sections.h2: The Anchor, the Crimea, and San Clemente
paras: Clement is named among the martyrs in the Roman Canon, but the details of his death come from a legendary Acts written in the fourth century or later. According to that account, Emperor Trajan exiled him to work in the mines near Chersonesus in the Crimea, where his preaching won converts, and he was then executed by being thrown into the Black Sea tied to an anchor. The anchor became his emblem in Christian art. Early historians such as Eusebius do not mention a martyrdom.

In the ninth century, Sts. Cyril and Methodius brought relics they believed to be Clement’s from the Crimea to Rome, where they were placed in the Basilica of San Clemente. That church, built over a fourth-century basilica and earlier Roman structures, remains a well-known pilgrimage site. Clement’s feast is November 23 in the Western Church.

keyFacts: Fourth bishop of Rome and one of the Apostolic Fathers
Author, by ancient testimony, of First Clement to the Church of Corinth (c. 96)
Tertullian reports he was ordained by St. Peter
Martyrdom by anchor in the Crimea comes from later legend
Relics brought to Rome by Sts. Cyril and Methodius; venerated at San Clemente
Named in the Roman Canon; feast day November 23

faqs.question: What is the First Letter of Clement about?
faqs.answer: It is a letter from the Church of Rome to the Church of Corinth, where some members had deposed their presbyters. It calls for repentance and peace and argues that ministers appointed in succession from the apostles should not be removed. Ancient writers attribute it to Clement, though the letter itself does not name him.

faqs.question: Why is St. Clement shown with an anchor?
faqs.answer: A later legend says he was exiled to the Crimea under Trajan and executed by being thrown into the sea tied to an anchor. The story is not found in the earliest sources, but the anchor became his traditional symbol.

faqs.question: Is Pope Clement I the Clement mentioned by St. Paul?
faqs.answer: Possibly. Origen and Eusebius identified him with the Clement whom Paul calls a co-worker in Philippians 4:3, but the name was common, and modern historians consider the link uncertain.

directAnswer: St. Evaristus was the fifth bishop of Rome, following Clement in the succession list of St. Irenaeus. The Liber Pontificalis describes him as a Greek, the son of a Jewish father from Bethlehem, and credits him with assigning Rome’s titular churches to priests. Apart from these traditions, nothing certain is known about him.

sections.h2: A Name in the Earliest Succession List
paras: Evaristus appears fourth after Peter in the list Irenaeus compiled around 180, and Eusebius repeats that order, giving him a pontificate of about eight years at the turn of the second century. That placement is the only early, reliable information we have.

The Liber Pontificalis, written several centuries later, says he was Greek by birth and that his father was a Jew from Bethlehem. If accurate, this would make him one of the earliest Roman bishops with Jewish roots after Peter, but the detail cannot be verified.

sections.h2: The Parish Tradition and Its Limits
paras: The same source credits Evaristus with dividing Rome’s titles, the house churches that later became parish churches, among the presbyters and with appointing deacons to assist the bishop. Historians generally see this as the compiler projecting later Roman church organization back onto an early pope, since the first-century community met in private homes without fixed districts.
Later tradition honors Evaristus as a martyr and holds that he was buried near St. Peter on the Vatican Hill, but there is no early account of his death. His feast is kept on October 26.

keyFacts: Fifth bishop of Rome, after Clement, in Irenaeus’s list
Liber Pontificalis calls him a Greek whose father was a Jew from Bethlehem
Traditionally credited with assigning Rome’s titular churches to priests
Honored as a martyr by later tradition; feast day October 26

faqs.question: Did Pope Evaristus really create the first parishes in Rome?
faqs.answer: The Liber Pontificalis says so, but historians doubt it. The structure of titular churches developed later, and the claim likely reflects the compiler’s own time rather than the early second century.

faqs.question: Was St. Evaristus Jewish?
faqs.answer: According to the Liber Pontificalis, his father was a Jew from Bethlehem, and he himself was Greek by birth. The source is late, so this family background is a tradition rather than a confirmed fact.

directAnswer: St. Alexander I was the sixth bishop of Rome, serving in the early second century after Evaristus. The Liber Pontificalis says he was a Roman and credits him with liturgical customs, including the use of water mixed with salt for blessing homes. These attributions come from much later sources, and few facts about his life are secure.

sections.h2: Holy Water and the Words of Institution
paras: Irenaeus lists Alexander fifth after Peter, and Eusebius dates his pontificate to roughly the reign of Emperor Trajan. Beyond this, our information comes from the Liber Pontificalis, which describes him as a Roman by birth.

That source credits him with two liturgical practices: adding the passage recalling the Lord’s Passion, beginning with the words on the night before he suffered, to the Eucharistic prayer, and introducing the blessing of water mixed with salt for sprinkling in homes. Historians regard both as later customs attached to an early name, though the association of Alexander with holy water has remained popular in Catholic devotion.

sections.h2: A Martyrdom Tradition Confused With Another Alexander
paras: Tradition long held that Pope Alexander was martyred and buried on the Via Nomentana with companions named Eventius and Theodulus. When a cemetery with the tombs of martyrs named Alexander, Eventius, and Theodulus was discovered on that road in the nineteenth century, scholars concluded that the Alexander buried there was most likely a different martyr, not the pope.
As a result, the circumstances of the pope’s death remain unknown. His traditional commemoration falls on May 3.

keyFacts: Sixth bishop of Rome, following Evaristus
Called a Roman by birth in the Liber Pontificalis
Traditionally credited with blessing homes with water mixed with salt
Martyrdom on the Via Nomentana likely belongs to another Alexander
Traditional commemoration: May 3

faqs.question: Did Pope Alexander I start the use of holy water?
faqs.answer: The Liber Pontificalis attributes to him the blessing of water mixed with salt for use in homes. Historians consider this a later tradition, but it explains why he is associated with holy water in Catholic devotion.

faqs.question: Was Pope Alexander I martyred?
faqs.answer: Tradition says so, but the martyr Alexander buried on the Via Nomentana with Eventius and Theodulus is now generally thought to be someone else. How the pope died is not known.

directAnswer: St. Sixtus I, also written Xystus, was the seventh bishop of Rome in the early second century. Irenaeus lists him sixth after the apostles, and the Liber Pontificalis attributes several liturgical rules to him. Little more is known, and the claim that he died a martyr is unverified.

paras: The original Greek form of his name was Xystus, and Irenaeus places him sixth from the apostles, a position that later writers noted as fitting the name. Eusebius gives him a pontificate of about ten years in the reign of Emperor Hadrian. He is the first of three popes to bear the name in the early Church, followed by the martyr Sixtus II and by Sixtus III in the fifth century.
The Liber Pontificalis describes him as a Roman, son of Pastor, which fits the note that he was of Greek descent but raised in Italy. The details cannot be confirmed.

Later sources credit Sixtus I with decreeing that only sacred ministers should touch the sacred vessels and that the people should join the celebrant in singing the Sanctus at Mass. As with other early popes, historians regard these as customs of later centuries that were assigned to an ancient name.
He is honored as a martyr, but no early account of his death exists. The town of Alatri, southeast of Rome, has long claimed to hold his relics. His traditional feast is April 6.

keyFacts: Seventh bishop of Rome; Greek name Xystus
Placed sixth after the apostles in Irenaeus’s list
Later sources credit him with rules on the sacred vessels and the Sanctus
Relics claimed by the town of Alatri, Italy
Traditional feast day: April 6

faqs.question: Is Pope Sixtus I the same as the St. Sixtus in the Mass?
faqs.answer: No. The Sixtus named in the Roman Canon is Sixtus II, who was beheaded in 258 during the persecution of Valerian. Sixtus I lived more than a century earlier.

faqs.question: What decrees are attributed to Pope Sixtus I?
faqs.answer: The Liber Pontificalis says he reserved the handling of sacred vessels to ministers and had the people sing the Sanctus with the priest. Historians think these attributions reflect later practice rather than his own legislation.

directAnswer: St. Telesphorus was the eighth bishop of Rome and the first pope after St. Peter whose martyrdom is attested by an early, reliable witness: St. Irenaeus wrote that he died gloriously as a martyr. Later tradition says he was Greek and credits him with Lenten and Christmas customs, though those attributions are uncertain.

paras: When Irenaeus listed the bishops of Rome around 180, he singled out only one of Peter’s early successors for martyrdom: Telesphorus, seventh after the apostles, who he said suffered a glorious martyrdom. Because Irenaeus wrote within a few decades of the event and had ties to the Roman Church, historians treat this as the earliest solid evidence for a papal martyrdom after Peter.
Eusebius places his death in the first year of Emperor Antoninus Pius, around 137 or 138, which agrees with the reign dates on this page. No account of how he died has survived.

The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Greek and a former anchorite, or hermit, and credits him with three customs: a seven-week fast before Easter, Mass celebrated at night on Christmas, and the singing of the Gloria at that Mass. Historians consider these later developments, since the feast of Christmas is not attested in Rome until the fourth century, but the attributions explain why Telesphorus is linked with these seasons.
His feast is traditionally kept on January 5, close to Christmas and Epiphany.

keyFacts: Eighth bishop of Rome, c. 125 to c. 138
Irenaeus records his glorious martyrdom, the first attested after Peter
Eusebius dates his death to the first year of Antoninus Pius
Later tradition credits him with Lenten fasting and a Christmas night Mass
Traditional feast day: January 5

faqs.question: How do we know Pope Telesphorus was a martyr?
faqs.answer: St. Irenaeus, writing around 180, explicitly says Telesphorus suffered a glorious martyrdom. That early testimony is far stronger than the evidence for most other second-century popes, whose martyrdoms rest on later tradition.

faqs.question: Did St. Telesphorus begin Midnight Mass at Christmas?
faqs.answer: The Liber Pontificalis attributes a nighttime Christmas Mass to him, but the celebration of Christmas itself is not documented in Rome until the fourth century. Historians see the attribution as a later tradition.

directAnswer: St. Hyginus was the ninth bishop of Rome, serving briefly around 138 to 142. Irenaeus records that the Gnostic teachers Valentinus and Cerdo came to Rome during his time, which shows the Roman Church facing its first major doctrinal challenges. Later tradition calls him a Greek philosopher from Athens, but little is known for certain.

sections.h2: Rome and the Arrival of the Gnostic Teachers
paras: Irenaeus notes that Valentinus, one of the most influential Gnostic teachers, came to Rome under Hyginus, and that Cerdo, a teacher who influenced Marcion, also came to the city in his time and moved in and out of the Church, at times confessing his errors and at times teaching them again. These remarks are the only reliable window onto Hyginus’s pontificate, and they suggest a period when the Roman Church was learning to deal with rival teachers in its midst.
How Hyginus himself responded is not recorded; the full rupture with Valentinus and Marcion came under his successors.

The Liber Pontificalis describes Hyginus as a Greek philosopher from Athens and credits him with organizing the ranks of the Roman clergy. Medieval tradition also linked him with the practice of having godparents at baptism. Neither claim can be confirmed from early sources.
He is honored as a martyr, though no early writer reports a martyrdom, and his feast is kept on January 11.

keyFacts: Ninth bishop of Rome, c. 138 to c. 142
Valentinus and Cerdo came to Rome in his time, according to Irenaeus
Liber Pontificalis calls him a Greek philosopher from Athens
Traditionally credited with organizing the clergy
Feast day: January 11

faqs.question: What challenges did the Church face under Pope Hyginus?
faqs.answer: Irenaeus records that the Gnostic teachers Valentinus and Cerdo arrived in Rome during his pontificate. Their teachings, which separated the God of the Old Testament from the Father of Jesus, became a serious challenge to the Roman Church in the following years.

faqs.question: Was Pope Hyginus martyred?
faqs.answer: Later tradition honors him as a martyr, but no early source mentions how he died, so his martyrdom is uncertain.

directAnswer: St. Pius I was the tenth bishop of Rome, serving in the mid-second century. An ancient document, the Muratorian Fragment, says he was the brother of Hermas, author of the early Christian work The Shepherd. His pontificate coincided with the activity of Marcion and Valentinus in Rome; most other details about him come from later tradition.

paras: The Muratorian Fragment, an early list of accepted Christian writings, states that Hermas wrote The Shepherd quite recently in Rome, while his brother Pius was occupying the chair of the Church of the city. This makes Pius one of the few early popes with a known relative and connects him with one of the most widely read Christian books of the second century, a work of visions and moral teaching that calls believers to repentance.
The Liber Pontificalis names Aquileia in northern Italy as his birthplace; that detail is less secure.

sections.h2: Marcion and the Question of Easter
paras: Pius led the Roman Church during a turbulent period. Marcion, who rejected the Old Testament and much of the New, was active in Rome around this time and broke with the Roman community, traditionally dated to about 144. Valentinus also continued teaching in the city. The sources do not describe Pius’s personal role in these events.

Later tradition credits him with decreeing that Easter be celebrated only on a Sunday, but this appears to read later controversies back into his reign. He is honored as a martyr, though early evidence for his martyrdom is lacking. His feast day is July 11.

keyFacts: Tenth bishop of Rome, c. 142 to c. 155
Brother of Hermas, author of The Shepherd, per the Muratorian Fragment
Marcion broke with the Roman Church during his pontificate
Liber Pontificalis names Aquileia as his birthplace
Feast day: July 11

faqs.question: Who was Hermas, the brother of Pope Pius I?
faqs.answer: Hermas was a Roman Christian who wrote The Shepherd, a book of visions, commandments, and parables on repentance that was widely read in the early Church. The Muratorian Fragment says he wrote it while his brother Pius was bishop of Rome.

faqs.question: Did Pope Pius I decide that Easter falls on Sunday?
faqs.answer: Later tradition says so, but there is no early evidence for such a decree. Roman Christians did keep Easter on Sunday in this period, and the formal dispute over the date came later under Popes Anicetus and Victor I.

directAnswer: St. Anicetus was the eleventh bishop of Rome, traditionally from Emesa in Syria and so remembered as the first Syrian pope. He is best known for receiving St. Polycarp of Smyrna, who came to Rome to discuss the date of Easter; the two disagreed but remained in full communion. The historian Hegesippus also visited Rome during his pontificate.

sections.h2: Polycarp’s Visit and the Easter Question
paras: The churches of Asia Minor celebrated the Pascha on the fourteenth day of the Jewish month of Nisan, whatever day of the week it fell, while Rome kept it on Sunday. St. Polycarp, the elderly bishop of Smyrna who had known the apostle John, traveled to Rome to discuss this and other matters with Anicetus. Irenaeus, who reports the meeting in a letter preserved by Eusebius, says neither could persuade the other to change his tradition.

Yet the two bishops parted in peace. According to Irenaeus, Anicetus yielded to Polycarp the celebration of the Eucharist in his own church as a mark of respect. Irenaeus later held up this episode as a model of unity amid differences when he urged Pope Victor I not to break communion over the same question.

Hegesippus, a Christian writer from the East, came to Rome while Anicetus was bishop and, by his own account, drew up a list of the Roman succession, noting that Eleutherus was then Anicetus’s deacon. His work survives only in fragments, but it shows how important the line of bishops already was as a guarantee of sound teaching.

The Liber Pontificalis describes Anicetus as a Syrian from Emesa and credits him with forbidding clergy to wear long hair. Later tradition honors him as a martyr, though early sources do not describe his death.

keyFacts: Eleventh bishop of Rome, c. 155 to c. 166
Traditionally from Emesa (modern Homs), Syria; called the first Syrian pope
Received St. Polycarp of Smyrna to discuss the date of Easter
Hegesippus compiled a Roman succession list during his pontificate
Honored as a martyr by later tradition

faqs.question: What happened when St. Polycarp met Pope Anicetus?
faqs.answer: They discussed the date of Easter, which Asian churches kept on the fourteenth of Nisan and Rome kept on Sunday. Neither changed his practice, but they stayed in communion, and Anicetus invited Polycarp to celebrate the Eucharist in Rome, according to St. Irenaeus.

faqs.question: Why is Anicetus called the first Syrian pope?
faqs.answer: The Liber Pontificalis says he came from Emesa in Syria. The source is late, but no earlier bishop of Rome is linked with Syria, so tradition counts him as the first.

directAnswer: St. Soter was the twelfth bishop of Rome, serving around 166 to 175. He is remembered chiefly through a letter of Bishop Dionysius of Corinth, who thanked the Roman Church under Soter for its generous aid to poor Christians and mentioned a letter Soter had sent to Corinth. The Liber Pontificalis says he came from Fondi in Campania.

sections.h2: Roman Charity in Dionysius of Corinth’s Letter
paras: Eusebius preserves part of a letter that Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, wrote to the Roman Church during Soter’s pontificate. Dionysius praises the Romans for a custom kept from the beginning of sending help to many churches and to Christians condemned to the mines, and he credits Soter with not only maintaining but increasing this generosity while encouraging visiting believers like a loving father.

Dionysius also says that his church read Soter’s letter aloud on the Lord’s Day, just as it still read the earlier letter sent through Clement. The text of Soter’s own letter is lost, but the exchange shows the Roman Church already in close, caring contact with communities far away.

The Liber Pontificalis names Fondi as Soter’s hometown and attributes disciplinary rules to him, and some later writers credited him with promoting the yearly celebration of Easter in Rome or with rules about the blessing of marriages. None of these claims rests on early evidence.
He is honored as a martyr in later tradition, and his feast has been kept on April 22, together with Pope St. Caius.

keyFacts: Twelfth bishop of Rome, c. 166 to c. 175
Praised by Dionysius of Corinth for Roman charity to distant churches
His letter to Corinth was read aloud at Sunday worship there
Liber Pontificalis says he came from Fondi, Campania
Traditional feast day April 22, shared with St. Caius

faqs.question: What do we actually know about Pope St. Soter?
faqs.answer: The most reliable evidence is a letter of Dionysius of Corinth, quoted by Eusebius, which praises the Roman Church under Soter for supporting poor Christians elsewhere and mentions a letter Soter sent to Corinth. Most other details come from later, less reliable sources.

faqs.question: Did Pope Soter write any letters?
faqs.answer: Yes, he wrote to the Church of Corinth, which read his letter at Sunday worship. The letter itself has not survived; we know of it only through Dionysius of Corinth’s reply.

directAnswer: St. Eleutherius (also Eleutherus) was the thirteenth bishop of Rome, serving around 175 to 189. He was bishop when St. Irenaeus wrote his famous succession list, and he received letters from the martyrs of Lyon about the Montanist movement. A later story that he sent missionaries to a British king named Lucius is considered legendary.

sections.h2: Irenaeus, the Martyrs of Lyon, and Montanism
paras: Hegesippus records that Eleutherius had served as a deacon under Pope Anicetus. By the time Irenaeus wrote Against Heresies, Eleutherius was bishop of Rome, and Irenaeus closes his list of Roman bishops with him, describing him as holding the office in the twelfth place from the apostles.

Around 177 the Christians of Lyon and Vienne in Gaul suffered a fierce persecution. Eusebius reports that the imprisoned confessors sent Irenaeus, then a presbyter, to Rome with letters for Eleutherius concerning the Montanist prophetic movement from Phrygia, and that their letters commended Irenaeus warmly. The episode shows churches in Gaul looking to Rome on a disputed question, though the exact content of their advice is debated.

sections.h2: The Legend of King Lucius of Britain
paras: The Liber Pontificalis says that Eleutherius received a letter from Lucius, a king of Britain, asking to become a Christian. The story was repeated by Bede and became part of British church legend, but historians regard it as unhistorical, perhaps arising from a confusion with a ruler of Edessa. The same source describes him as a Greek from Nicopolis in Epirus.
Later tradition honors Eleutherius as a martyr, but early writers do not record his death as a martyrdom.

keyFacts: Thirteenth bishop of Rome, c. 175 to c. 189
Earlier a deacon under Pope Anicetus, according to Hegesippus
The last pope named in Irenaeus’s succession list
Received letters from the confessors of Lyon about Montanism
Liber Pontificalis calls him a Greek from Nicopolis in Epirus

faqs.question: Did Pope Eleutherius send missionaries to Britain?
faqs.answer: A story in the Liber Pontificalis, later repeated by Bede, says a British king named Lucius asked him for instruction in the faith. Historians generally regard this as a legend, possibly based on a misreading of a reference to a ruler elsewhere.

faqs.question: What was Pope Eleutherius’s connection to St. Irenaeus?
faqs.answer: Irenaeus carried letters from the persecuted Christians of Lyon to Eleutherius around 177, and Irenaeus’s list of Roman bishops in Against Heresies ends with Eleutherius as the current bishop.

directAnswer: St. Victor I was the fourteenth bishop of Rome and the first pope born in Africa. He is best known for the Easter controversy, in which he tried to cut off the churches of Asia Minor that celebrated Easter on the fourteenth of Nisan, and for excommunicating Theodotus the Tanner, an early adoptionist. St. Jerome counted him among the first Christian authors to write in Latin.

paras: The Liber Pontificalis records that Victor was an African, and he is generally regarded as the first bishop of Rome from that continent. Jerome, in his catalog of Christian writers, mentions Victor as having written short works in Latin, at a time when the Roman Church still worshiped and wrote mainly in Greek. This has made him a symbol of the Roman Church’s gradual turn toward Latin.
His pontificate fell under Emperor Commodus and the early years of Septimius Severus, a period of relative calm for Christians in Rome.

Christians in the Roman province of Asia, led by Bishop Polycrates of Ephesus, kept the Pascha on the fourteenth day of Nisan, the date of the Jewish Passover, whatever the day of the week. Rome and most other churches celebrated it on the following Sunday. Earlier, Anicetus and Polycarp had agreed to differ, but Victor pressed for a common practice.

Eusebius reports that synods met in Palestine, Pontus, Gaul, Osrhoene, and elsewhere, and agreed that the Resurrection should be celebrated only on Sunday. Polycrates replied with a firm letter defending the tradition he had received from the apostles John and Philip. Victor then sought to declare the Asian churches cut off from communion.

Several bishops objected to this severity. Irenaeus of Lyons, though he agreed with Sunday observance, wrote to Victor urging peace and reminding him how earlier Roman bishops had stayed in communion with those who kept a different custom. Eusebius’s account suggests Victor did not carry the matter to a complete break. Sunday observance eventually prevailed throughout the Church, and the Council of Nicaea in 325 settled a common date.

sections.h2: Theodotus the Tanner and the Prisoners in Sardinia
paras: Victor also confronted a doctrinal threat. Theodotus, a leather worker from Byzantium living in Rome, taught that Jesus was a mere man on whom the Spirit descended at baptism. According to a third-century writer quoted by Eusebius, Victor excommunicated him, one of the first recorded actions by a Roman bishop against an adoptionist teaching.

Hippolytus records another episode: Marcia, a woman close to Commodus, asked Victor for a list of Christians condemned to the mines of Sardinia and obtained their release. Among those freed was Callixtus, a future pope. Victor was later honored as a martyr, though early sources do not describe his death; his feast is kept on July 28.

keyFacts: Fourteenth bishop of Rome, c. 189 to 199; first pope born in Africa
Pressed the churches of Asia to keep Easter on Sunday (Quartodeciman controversy)
Rebuked for severity by St. Irenaeus, who urged peace
Excommunicated Theodotus the Tanner, an adoptionist
Provided the list that freed Christian prisoners, including Callixtus, from the Sardinian mines
Feast day: July 28

faqs.question: What was the Easter controversy under Pope Victor I?
faqs.answer: The churches of Asia Minor kept Easter on the fourteenth of Nisan, while Rome kept it on Sunday. Victor called for synods, which supported Sunday, and moved to break communion with the Asian churches. St. Irenaeus and other bishops urged him toward peace, and the question was finally settled for the whole Church at Nicaea in 325.

faqs.question: Was Pope Victor I the first pope from Africa?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Liber Pontificalis calls him an African, and he is generally counted as the first of the three popes from Africa, followed later by Miltiades and Gelasius I.

faqs.question: Did Pope Victor I make Latin the language of the Church?
faqs.answer: Not formally. St. Jerome mentions that Victor wrote in Latin, which makes him one of the earliest Latin Christian writers, but the Roman liturgy remained mostly Greek for well over a century after him.

directAnswer: St. Zephyrinus was the fifteenth bishop of Rome, leading the Church for nearly two decades from about 199 to 217. His pontificate was troubled by disputes over the nature of Christ, both from adoptionists who called Jesus a mere man and from teachers who blurred the distinction between Father and Son. His deacon Callixtus, the future pope, managed the Christian cemetery on the Appian Way.

sections.h2: Adoptionists, Modalists, and the Confessor Natalius
paras: Followers of Theodotus the Tanner, led by Theodotus the banker and Asclepiodotus, set up a rival community in Rome and even paid a confessor named Natalius to serve as their bishop. An anonymous work quoted by Eusebius says Natalius later repented and threw himself in tears at the feet of Zephyrinus, who received him back into communion.

At the same time, teachers such as Sabellius were spreading the idea that Father and Son were simply different modes of one divine person. Hippolytus, a learned Roman presbyter who became a bitter critic, accused Zephyrinus of being unlearned and too lenient toward these views. Because Hippolytus is hostile, historians read his portrait with caution.

sections.h2: Callixtus and the Cemetery on the Appian Way
paras: Zephyrinus made Callixtus, a former slave who had returned from the Sardinian mines, his chief deacon and put him in charge of a cemetery on the Via Appia. That cemetery, now the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, became the burial place of many third-century popes.

Eusebius also notes that Origen visited Rome during Zephyrinus’s time, wishing to see the ancient Church of the Romans. Later tradition calls Zephyrinus a martyr for his sufferings, though he does not seem to have died by violence. His feast is December 20.

keyFacts: Fifteenth bishop of Rome, c. 199 to 217
Opposed the adoptionist circle of Theodotus the banker and Asclepiodotus
Received back the repentant confessor Natalius
Appointed the deacon Callixtus to oversee the cemetery on the Via Appia
Origen visited Rome during his pontificate; feast day December 20

faqs.question: Why did Hippolytus criticize Pope Zephyrinus?
faqs.answer: Hippolytus accused him of being uneducated, easily influenced by his deacon Callixtus, and too tolerant of teachers who confused the Father and the Son. These charges come from a strongly partisan source, so historians treat them carefully.

faqs.question: Was Pope Zephyrinus a martyr?
faqs.answer: He is traditionally called a martyr because of the trials he endured, but there is no evidence that he was executed.

directAnswer: St. Callixtus I (also Callistus) was the sixteenth bishop of Rome, a former slave who rose to become chief deacon under Pope Zephyrinus and then pope from about 217 to 222. He is known for a merciful policy toward repentant sinners, for his conflict with the rigorist Hippolytus, and for the Catacomb of St. Callixtus that bears his name. Tradition holds that he died a martyr.

sections.h2: From Slave to the Sardinian Mines
paras: Most of what we know about Callixtus’s early life comes from his opponent Hippolytus, whose account is hostile but detailed. He says Callixtus was the slave of a Christian named Carpophorus and managed a banking business that failed, after which he was punished and later condemned to the mines of Sardinia following a disturbance at a synagogue.

He was released when Marcia, a woman close to Emperor Commodus, obtained the freedom of Christian prisoners from a list supplied by Pope Victor I. Callixtus then lived at Antium on a pension until Zephyrinus called him back to Rome.

sections.h2: Deacon of the Catacomb on the Appian Way
paras: Zephyrinus made Callixtus his principal deacon and placed him in charge of a Christian burial ground on the Via Appia. Under his care it grew into the first official cemetery of the Roman Church, with a crypt where many third-century popes were later buried.

Today the Catacomb of St. Callixtus is one of the most visited Christian sites in Rome. Ironically, Callixtus himself was not buried there; his tomb was in the cemetery of Calepodius on the Via Aurelia.

sections.h2: Mercy for Sinners and the Schism of Hippolytus
paras: When Zephyrinus died, Callixtus was chosen bishop. Hippolytus refused to accept him and led a separate community, and he is often counted as the first antipope. In his Refutation of All Heresies, Hippolytus attacks Callixtus for receiving back Christians guilty of serious sins after penance, for not deposing clergy who had married more than once, and for recognizing unions between Christian women of high rank and men of lower status that Roman law did not allow.

Seen from the other side, these complaints describe a bishop who held that the Church has power to forgive grave sins and who adapted discipline to pastoral need. Callixtus also condemned Sabellius, whose teaching dissolved the distinction between Father and Son. Hippolytus nonetheless charged him with leaning toward error, a charge most historians regard as partisan.

Callixtus is venerated as a martyr. A later account says he was killed during a popular uprising in Trastevere and thrown into a well, but that story is legendary, and the exact circumstances of his death are unknown since no general persecution was under way. He is associated with the area of Santa Maria in Trastevere, and his feast is October 14.
Hippolytus was later reconciled to the Church and died a martyr alongside Pope Pontian, so both men who once opposed each other are honored as saints.

keyFacts: Sixteenth bishop of Rome, c. 217 to 222
Former slave, later condemned to the Sardinian mines and released
As deacon, oversaw the cemetery now called the Catacomb of St. Callixtus
Opposed by Hippolytus, often counted as the first antipope
Defended the Church’s power to forgive grave sins after penance
Buried on the Via Aurelia; feast day October 14

faqs.question: Is Pope St. Callixtus buried in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus?
faqs.answer: No. Although the catacomb is named for him because he managed it as a deacon, he was buried in the cemetery of Calepodius on the Via Aurelia.

faqs.question: Why did Hippolytus oppose Pope Callixtus?
faqs.answer: Hippolytus thought Callixtus was too lenient, especially in readmitting serious sinners after penance, and accused him of doctrinal error. He set up a rival community, but he was later reconciled and died a martyr.

faqs.question: How did Pope Callixtus I die?
faqs.answer: He is honored as a martyr. A later tradition says he was killed in a riot in Trastevere and thrown into a well, but that account is legendary, and the real circumstances are not known.

directAnswer: St. Urban I was the seventeenth bishop of Rome, serving from about 222 to 230 during the reign of Emperor Alexander Severus, a time of relative peace for Christians. Reliable information about his pontificate is very scarce. A later legend makes him the pope who baptized the husband of St. Cecilia.

sections.h2: A Peaceful Pontificate Under Alexander Severus
paras: Eusebius records only that Urban succeeded Callixtus and held office for about eight years. His time as bishop fell under Alexander Severus, an emperor generally tolerant toward Christians, so the Roman Church seems to have enjoyed a period of calm.
The schism of Hippolytus, which began under Callixtus, likely continued during Urban’s pontificate, but no source describes how he dealt with it.

sections.h2: Urban in the Legend of St. Cecilia
paras: Urban is best known today through the Acts of St. Cecilia, a later and largely legendary account in which a Bishop Urban instructs and baptizes Valerian, Cecilia’s husband, and his brother Tiburtius. Historians doubt whether this Urban was the pope, and the story cannot be used as a source for his life.

A gravestone inscribed with the Greek name Ourbanos was found in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, but scholars debate whether it marks the pope’s tomb. He is honored as a saint, and his feast is May 25.

keyFacts: Seventeenth bishop of Rome, c. 222 to 230
Reigned under Emperor Alexander Severus, a time of relative peace
Appears in the legendary Acts of St. Cecilia
Burial place debated; an Ourbanos inscription exists in the papal crypt
Feast day: May 25

faqs.question: Did Pope Urban I baptize St. Cecilia’s husband?
faqs.answer: The Acts of St. Cecilia say a Bishop Urban baptized her husband, Valerian. Those Acts are largely legendary, so historians cannot confirm that the pope was involved.

faqs.question: Was Pope Urban I martyred?
faqs.answer: Later tradition says so, but his pontificate fell in a peaceful period, and there is no early evidence that he died for the faith.

directAnswer: St. Pontian was the eighteenth bishop of Rome, from 230 to 235, and the first pope known to have resigned. Exiled to the mines of Sardinia by Emperor Maximinus Thrax, he stepped down on September 28, 235, the earliest exact date in papal history, and died in exile. Tradition holds that he was reconciled there with Hippolytus, the former rival bishop.

sections.h2: Exile to Sardinia and the First Papal Resignation
paras: The Liberian Catalogue, a list of Roman bishops compiled in the fourth century, records that Pontian and the presbyter Hippolytus were deported to Sardinia, an island with a notoriously deadly mining colony, and that Pontian resigned on September 28, 235. The resignation allowed the Roman Church to elect a successor rather than remain leaderless while its bishop was in exile.

The exile came early in the reign of Maximinus Thrax, who reversed the tolerance of his predecessor and targeted Church leaders. Pontian died in Sardinia soon after, probably from the harsh conditions.

Hippolytus had led a separate community since the time of Callixtus. Their shared exile seems to have ended the division, and both men are honored as martyrs. According to Jerome, Pontian had also held a Roman synod that endorsed the condemnation of Origen by Bishop Demetrius of Alexandria.

Pope Fabian later had Pontian’s body brought back to Rome and buried in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, where fragments of his Greek epitaph were later discovered. Pontian and Hippolytus share a feast day on August 13.

keyFacts: Eighteenth bishop of Rome, July 21, 230, to September 28, 235
Exiled to Sardinia under Emperor Maximinus Thrax
First pope known to have resigned, on September 28, 235
Reconciled with Hippolytus, who shared his exile
Buried in the papal crypt of St. Callixtus; feast day August 13

faqs.question: Why did Pope St. Pontian resign?
faqs.answer: He was exiled to the mines of Sardinia, where he could not lead the Church. By resigning on September 28, 235, he allowed Rome to elect a new bishop. He died in exile shortly afterward.

faqs.question: Why do Pontian and Hippolytus share a feast day?
faqs.answer: Hippolytus had opposed earlier popes and led a rival community, but he and Pontian were exiled together to Sardinia. Tradition holds that they were reconciled there, and both are venerated as martyrs on August 13.

directAnswer: St. Anterus was the nineteenth bishop of Rome and one of the shortest-reigning popes, serving only about six weeks from November 21, 235, to January 3, 236. He succeeded Pontian, who had resigned in exile. His Greek epitaph survives in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, but almost nothing else is known.

paras: Anterus was elected after Pontian resigned in Sardinia, during the hostile reign of Maximinus Thrax. The Liberian Catalogue records that he died on January 3, 236, after barely more than a month in office.

The Liber Pontificalis says he was a Greek and claims he collected the official records of the martyrs, and that this led to his own martyrdom. Historians doubt this story, since it seems designed to explain a short reign, and the early lists do not call him a martyr.

sections.h2: The Epitaph in the Papal Crypt
paras: Anterus was the first pope buried in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus. In 1854, the archaeologist Giovanni Battista de Rossi found fragments of his tombstone there with his name and the title of bishop in Greek. It remains the most tangible trace of his life. His feast is January 3.

keyFacts: Nineteenth bishop of Rome, November 21, 235, to January 3, 236
One of the shortest pontificates in the early Church
Liber Pontificalis calls him Greek and credits him with collecting martyrs’ acts
First pope buried in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus
Feast day: January 3

faqs.question: How long was Pope St. Anterus pope?
faqs.answer: About six weeks. He was elected on November 21, 235, and died on January 3, 236.

faqs.question: Was Pope Anterus a martyr?
faqs.answer: The Liber Pontificalis says he was martyred for collecting the acts of the martyrs, but the earlier Liberian Catalogue simply records his death. Historians regard the martyrdom as uncertain.

directAnswer: St. Fabian was the twentieth bishop of Rome, from 236 to 250. A layman when chosen, he was elected after a dove reportedly landed on his head, according to the historian Eusebius. He reorganized the Roman Church into seven districts under deacons, brought back the body of Pope Pontian from Sardinia, and died a martyr on January 20, 250, in the persecution of Emperor Decius.

paras: Eusebius tells how, after the death of Anterus, the Christians of Rome gathered to choose a bishop. Fabian, a layman who had recently come in from the countryside, was not considered a likely candidate. Then a dove came down and settled on his head, and the assembly, seeing a sign like the Spirit’s descent at Christ’s baptism, acclaimed him bishop and placed him on the episcopal chair.
The story, written down about a century later, may be embellished, but it reflects the high regard in which Fabian was held and the custom of the whole community taking part in the election.

According to the Liberian Catalogue and the Liber Pontificalis, Fabian divided the city into seven ecclesiastical regions, each entrusted to a deacon who cared for the poor and the cemeteries. He is also said to have appointed subdeacons and notaries to record the acts of the martyrs. The number seven echoes the deacons chosen in Acts 6.

Fabian oversaw building work in the catacombs and arranged for the body of Pontian, who had died in Sardinia, to be brought back and buried in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus. These reforms gave the growing Roman Church a structure that lasted for centuries.

Fabian’s influence extended beyond Rome. Eusebius reports that Origen wrote to Fabian defending his own orthodoxy. Cyprian of Carthage referred to the condemnation of a heretical African bishop, Privatus, which had been confirmed by Fabian.
The long years of peace under emperors who tolerated Christianity allowed the Roman Church to grow under his leadership.

In 250, Emperor Decius ordered all inhabitants of the empire to offer sacrifice to the gods and obtain a certificate proving it. Fabian was among the first victims, dying on January 20, 250. After his death the Roman clergy wrote to Cyprian about it, and Cyprian, in his reply, praised the integrity of his life and death.

His tombstone, inscribed in Greek with his name, the word bishop, and an abbreviation for martyr, was found in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus. The persecution was so severe that the Roman Church could not elect a successor for more than a year. Fabian shares his feast day, January 20, with St. Sebastian.

keyFacts: Twentieth bishop of Rome, January 10, 236, to January 20, 250
Elected as a layman after a dove settled on his head, according to Eusebius
Organized Rome into seven districts, each under a deacon
Brought Pope Pontian’s body back from Sardinia
Martyred in the persecution of Decius; tomb found in the papal crypt of St. Callixtus
Feast day: January 20, shared with St. Sebastian

faqs.question: How was Pope St. Fabian chosen?
faqs.answer: According to Eusebius, Fabian was a layman present at the election when a dove landed on his head. The assembly took it as a sign from the Holy Spirit and chose him unanimously.

faqs.question: How did Pope Fabian die?
faqs.answer: He was martyred on January 20, 250, at the start of the persecution under Emperor Decius, which required everyone to sacrifice to the Roman gods. St. Cyprian praised his faithful death.

faqs.question: Why do St. Fabian and St. Sebastian share a feast day?
faqs.answer: Both were Roman martyrs whose deaths were commemorated on January 20. Their feasts have long been celebrated together on that date.

directAnswer: St. Cornelius was the twenty-first bishop of Rome, elected in March 251 after the Church had gone more than a year without a bishop during the Decian persecution. His pontificate was defined by the controversy over readmitting Christians who had lapsed under persecution, in which he upheld reconciliation after penance against the rigorist Novatian. Exiled by Emperor Gallus, he died at Centumcellae in 253 and is honored as a martyr.

paras: After Pope Fabian was martyred in January 250, the persecution of Decius made it impossible for the Roman Church to choose a successor, and the presbyters governed collectively for over a year. When the pressure eased, Cornelius was elected in March 251. St. Cyprian of Carthage later wrote that he had risen through all the ranks of the clergy and had not sought the office, but accepted it under pressure.

His election was immediately challenged. Novatian, a gifted Roman presbyter and theologian who had written an important treatise on the Trinity, had himself consecrated as a rival bishop and is counted among the antipopes.

sections.h2: The Lapsed and the Schism of Novatian
paras: The central issue was how to treat the lapsed, Christians who had offered sacrifice or bought certificates to escape punishment under Decius. Novatian held that the Church could not grant them reconciliation; only God could forgive them. Cornelius, in agreement with Cyprian and most bishops, held that they could be received back after suitable penance.

Cornelius convened a synod in Rome of about sixty bishops, which condemned Novatian and his followers and confirmed the policy of readmitting the repentant. Synods in Africa and elsewhere took the same line. Novatian’s community nonetheless survived as a separate church for several centuries.

Cyprian at first hesitated to recognize Cornelius until he was sure of the facts, then became his firm supporter. Their surviving correspondence is one of the richest sources for the Church of the mid-third century and for relations between Rome and Carthage.

sections.h2: A Snapshot of the Roman Church
paras: In a letter to Bishop Fabius of Antioch, preserved by Eusebius, Cornelius describes the clergy of Rome to show how absurd it was for Novatian to claim the office. He lists forty-six presbyters, seven deacons, seven subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers, and says the Church supported more than fifteen hundred widows and people in distress.
These figures make the letter one of the most valuable records of how a major Christian community was organized before Constantine, and they suggest a Roman Church numbering many thousands.

In 252, under Emperor Trebonianus Gallus, persecution resumed and Cornelius was banished to Centumcellae, the port now called Civitavecchia. Cyprian wrote to congratulate him on his steadfast confession. Cornelius died there in June 253, and the Church regards his death from the hardships of exile as martyrdom.

His body was later brought to Rome and buried in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, in a separate crypt where his tomb bears a Latin inscription naming him a martyr. He is named in the Roman Canon, and his feast is kept on September 16 together with St. Cyprian.

keyFacts: Twenty-first bishop of Rome, March 6, 251, to June 253
Upheld reconciliation of the lapsed after penance against Novatian
Roman synod of about sixty bishops condemned Novatian
His letter to Fabius of Antioch records the size of the Roman clergy
Died in exile at Centumcellae (Civitavecchia); buried in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus
Named in the Roman Canon; feast day September 16 with St. Cyprian

faqs.question: What was the Novatian schism?
faqs.answer: Novatian, a Roman presbyter, opposed Pope Cornelius’s policy of readmitting Christians who had lapsed during persecution, insisting the Church had no power to reconcile them. He was consecrated as a rival bishop and condemned by a Roman synod, but his rigorist church survived for centuries.

faqs.question: Why are St. Cornelius and St. Cyprian celebrated together?
faqs.answer: Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, supported Cornelius against Novatian, and they corresponded closely. Both died for the faith within a few years of each other, and the Church honors them together on September 16.

faqs.question: Was Pope Cornelius killed for his faith?
faqs.answer: He was not executed. He was exiled to Centumcellae under Emperor Gallus and died there in 253, and the Church honors his death in exile as martyrdom.

directAnswer: St. Lucius I was the twenty-second bishop of Rome, serving from June 253 to March 254. He was exiled soon after his election but allowed to return, and St. Cyprian of Carthage wrote to congratulate him. He continued Pope Cornelius’s policy of readmitting the lapsed after penance.

paras: Lucius was elected in June 253 after Cornelius died in exile. Under Emperor Gallus he too was banished, but he was soon permitted to come back to Rome, probably after Gallus fell from power. Cyprian of Carthage sent him a warm letter rejoicing at his return and praising him as a confessor who had shared in the sufferings of his predecessor.

Cyprian later wrote that Lucius, like Cornelius, had supported readmitting repentant Christians who had lapsed in persecution, so Lucius stood firmly on the side of mercy against the followers of Novatian.
Lucius died in March 254 after only about eight months in office. He was buried in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, where part of his tombstone with his name in Greek has been found.

The Liber Pontificalis claims he was beheaded under Valerian, but this conflicts with the dates, since Valerian’s persecution began several years later. Lucius is honored as a saint, and his feast is kept in early March.

keyFacts: Twenty-second bishop of Rome, June 25, 253, to March 5, 254
Exiled under Emperor Gallus and allowed to return to Rome
Received a congratulatory letter from St. Cyprian
Supported readmitting the lapsed after penance
Buried in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus

faqs.question: Was Pope Lucius I a martyr?
faqs.answer: He suffered exile and was praised by St. Cyprian as a confessor. The Liber Pontificalis says he was beheaded, but that account does not fit the timeline, and he likely died a natural death after returning to Rome.

faqs.question: Where is Pope St. Lucius I buried?
faqs.answer: In the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus on the Appian Way, where fragments of his Greek epitaph have been found.

directAnswer: St. Stephen I was the twenty-third bishop of Rome, from 254 to 257. He is best known for his dispute with St. Cyprian of Carthage over baptism administered by heretics: Stephen held that such baptisms were valid and should not be repeated, a position the Church later confirmed. Tradition says he was beheaded in the persecution of Valerian, though early sources do not clearly support this.

paras: In North Africa and parts of Asia Minor, converts from heretical or schismatic groups such as the Novatianists were baptized again, because those churches held that baptism outside the Catholic Church was invalid. Rome followed an older custom of receiving such converts by the laying on of hands for penance, without repeating baptism.

Cyprian and synods in Carthage defended rebaptism and wrote to Stephen. According to Cyprian, Stephen insisted that nothing should be innovated beyond what had been handed down, and he threatened to break communion with those who rebaptized. Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, sided with Cyprian and wrote a harsh letter against Stephen that survives among Cyprian’s correspondence.

Stephen’s pontificate also shows Rome being drawn into other churches’ affairs. Cyprian urged him to act against Marcian, bishop of Arles, who had joined the Novatianist position and refused reconciliation to the repentant. Two Spanish bishops, Basilides and Martial, who had been deposed for lapsing, appealed to Stephen and were restored, prompting the Spanish churches to seek Cyprian’s advice instead.
These episodes reveal a bishop of Rome who saw himself as having responsibility beyond his city, and other bishops who did not always agree with how he used it.

The dispute was not resolved during Stephen’s lifetime, and peace between Rome and Carthage was restored under his successor, Sixtus II. In the following century, the Council of Arles in 314 and later theology, especially that of St. Augustine, affirmed Stephen’s principle that baptism given with water in the name of the Trinity is valid even when performed by heretics, and so must not be repeated.
This remains Catholic teaching today and is why the Church recognizes the baptisms of many other Christian communities.

A later legend says Stephen was beheaded while seated on his episcopal chair in the catacombs during the persecution of Valerian. Many historians think this story was borrowed from the martyrdom of his successor, Sixtus II, since the Liberian Catalogue and the earliest Roman calendars do not list Stephen as a martyr.
His resting place was the crypt of the popes in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, and the Church keeps his feast on August 2.

keyFacts: Twenty-third bishop of Rome, May 12, 254, to August 2, 257
Taught that baptism given by heretics is valid and must not be repeated
Clashed with St. Cyprian of Carthage and Firmilian of Caesarea
Received appeals from bishops in Spain and concerns about Arles in Gaul
Martyrdom by beheading is a later tradition; buried in the papal crypt of St. Callixtus
Feast day: August 2

faqs.question: What was the rebaptism controversy?
faqs.answer: It was a dispute over whether converts baptized in heretical or schismatic groups needed to be baptized again. St. Cyprian said yes; Pope Stephen I said no, holding that a baptism given properly in the name of the Trinity is valid. The Church later adopted Stephen’s view.

faqs.question: Was Pope Stephen I really beheaded on his chair?
faqs.answer: That is a later tradition. Several early Roman lists do not call him a martyr, and historians suspect the story was transferred from Pope Sixtus II, who was executed in the catacombs in 258.

faqs.question: Did Pope Stephen I and St. Cyprian ever reconcile?
faqs.answer: Not during Stephen’s life. Peace was restored under his successor, Sixtus II, and both Stephen and Cyprian are honored as saints.

directAnswer: St. Sixtus II was the twenty-fourth bishop of Rome, serving for less than a year before he was beheaded on August 6, 258, during the persecution of Emperor Valerian. He restored peace with the churches of Africa and Asia after the rebaptism dispute and was arrested while presiding over a gathering in a Roman cemetery. He is one of the most revered early martyrs and is named in the Roman Canon.

sections.h2: A Peacemaker After the Rebaptism Dispute
paras: Sixtus, whose name is written Xystus in Greek and Latin sources, was elected in August 257 after the death of Stephen I. Stephen had come close to breaking communion with Cyprian of Carthage and the bishops of Asia over rebaptism. Sixtus appears to have kept Rome’s position while restoring friendly relations.

Pontius, the deacon who wrote the life of Cyprian, called Sixtus a good and peaceable priest, and Dionysius of Alexandria wrote to him on the baptism question in a conciliatory spirit. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Greek, but that detail may result from confusion with a philosopher of the same name.

sections.h2: Valerian’s Edict and the Arrest in the Catacomb
paras: In 257 Emperor Valerian ordered clergy to sacrifice to the gods and forbade Christians to meet in their cemeteries. In 258 a harsher edict ordered that bishops, priests, and deacons be executed. Cyprian, in a letter written shortly before his own martyrdom, reported that Xystus had been put to death in a cemetery on August 6 together with four deacons.

According to tradition, soldiers found Sixtus seated in his chair addressing the faithful in the Catacomb of Praetextatus on the Appian Way and executed him there. Other deacons of his were martyred the same day, and his archdeacon St. Lawrence was put to death a few days later, on August 10.

Sixtus was buried in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, which became a major pilgrimage site because of him. In the fourth century, Pope Damasus composed a verse inscription for the crypt honoring the martyred bishop who had been teaching his flock when the soldiers came.

He was one of the most widely venerated Roman martyrs of antiquity, and his name appears in the Roman Canon alongside Cornelius and Cyprian. Because August 6 is the Feast of the Transfiguration, the Church celebrates Sixtus II and his companions on August 7.

keyFacts: Twenty-fourth bishop of Rome, August 31, 257, to August 6, 258
Restored peace with Carthage and the Eastern churches after the rebaptism dispute
Beheaded with deacons during Valerian’s persecution, as reported by St. Cyprian
His archdeacon St. Lawrence was martyred four days later
Buried in the papal crypt of St. Callixtus; honored by an inscription of Pope Damasus
Named in the Roman Canon; memorial on August 7

faqs.question: How did Pope St. Sixtus II die?
faqs.answer: He was executed on August 6, 258, under the edict of Emperor Valerian against Christian clergy. St. Cyprian reported that he was put to death in a cemetery with four deacons, and tradition places his arrest in the Catacomb of Praetextatus.

faqs.question: What was the connection between Sixtus II and St. Lawrence?
faqs.answer: Lawrence was one of Sixtus’s deacons and the chief administrator of the Roman Church’s goods. He was martyred on August 10, 258, a few days after Sixtus.

faqs.question: Why is the feast of St. Sixtus II on August 7?
faqs.answer: He died on August 6, but that date is the Feast of the Transfiguration. The Church therefore keeps the memorial of Sixtus II and his companions on August 7.

directAnswer: St. Dionysius was the twenty-fifth bishop of Rome, elected in 259 after a vacancy caused by the persecution of Valerian. He rebuilt the Roman Church once Emperor Gallienus ended the persecution, corresponded with Dionysius of Alexandria on how to speak about the Trinity, and sent aid to Christians in Cappadocia taken captive by raiders. His pontificate lasted until his death in December 268.

paras: After Sixtus II was executed in 258, the Roman Church went without a bishop for nearly a year. Dionysius, a presbyter, was elected in July 259. In 260, Valerian was captured by the Persians, and his son Gallienus issued an edict that restored property to Christians and ended the persecution, beginning about forty years of relative peace.
The Liber Pontificalis credits Dionysius with reorganizing the city’s churches and cemeteries, which would fit the needs of this recovery period, though the details are uncertain.

sections.h2: The Two Dionysii and the Language of the Trinity
paras: Some Christians in Libya complained to Rome that Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria, in fighting Sabellianism, had spoken of the Son as if he were a creature separate from the Father. Pope Dionysius held a synod in Rome and wrote a letter, part of which St. Athanasius later preserved, rejecting both the Sabellian merging of Father and Son and any division of God into separate powers. The Alexandrian bishop replied with a defense explaining his meaning.

Historians see this exchange as an important step toward the vocabulary later defined at Nicaea. Dionysius also sent a letter and money to the church of Caesarea in Cappadocia to ransom captives taken by invaders, a gesture still remembered there a century later by St. Basil. He is honored as a saint, with a feast day of December 26.

keyFacts: Twenty-fifth bishop of Rome, July 22, 259, to December 26, 268
Elected after a vacancy caused by the persecution of Valerian
Led the Church after Gallienus’s edict ended the persecution in 260
Corresponded with Dionysius of Alexandria on Trinitarian doctrine
Sent aid to ransom Christian captives in Cappadocia

faqs.question: What was the dispute between Pope Dionysius and Dionysius of Alexandria?
faqs.answer: Critics accused the bishop of Alexandria of speaking of the Son as a creature separate from the Father. Pope Dionysius held a Roman synod and wrote a letter rejecting both that error and Sabellianism, and the Alexandrian bishop clarified his teaching in reply.

faqs.question: Was Pope Dionysius a martyr?
faqs.answer: No. He governed the Church during a time of peace after Emperor Gallienus ended the persecution, and he is honored as a saint rather than as a martyr.

directAnswer: St. Felix I was the twenty-sixth bishop of Rome, serving from 269 to 274. His pontificate is linked with the case of Paul of Samosata, the deposed bishop of Antioch, whose removal Emperor Aurelian enforced in favor of the bishop recognized by the bishops of Italy and Rome. Little else is known for certain about him.

sections.h2: Paul of Samosata and the Emperor’s Ruling
paras: A synod at Antioch in 268 deposed its bishop, Paul of Samosata, for teaching that Jesus was a man inspired by the divine Word rather than the Word made flesh. The synod sent a letter to Rome announcing the decision, addressed to Pope Dionysius, who had died by the time it arrived, so it fell to Felix to receive it.

Paul refused to give up the church house in Antioch. Eusebius reports that Christians appealed to Emperor Aurelian, who ruled that the building should belong to those with whom the bishops of Italy and of Rome were in communion. This decision, made by a pagan emperor, is an early sign that communion with Rome was recognized as a mark of legitimacy.

sections.h2: A Disputed Letter and Later Traditions
paras: A letter about the Incarnation attributed to Felix was cited at the Council of Ephesus in 431, but scholars now regard it as a forgery by followers of Apollinaris. The Liber Pontificalis credits Felix with the practice of celebrating Mass over the tombs of martyrs and calls him a martyr himself; historians doubt both claims, since his reign fell in a period of peace.
Early Roman records place his burial in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus. His feast is December 30.

keyFacts: Twenty-sixth bishop of Rome, January 5, 269, to December 30, 274
Received the synod of Antioch’s announcement of Paul of Samosata’s deposition
Emperor Aurelian sided with the bishop in communion with Rome
A letter cited at Ephesus in his name is now considered an Apollinarian forgery
Feast day: December 30

faqs.question: Why is Pope Felix I connected with Emperor Aurelian?
faqs.answer: When the deposed bishop Paul of Samosata refused to leave the church property in Antioch, Aurelian ruled that it belonged to the bishop in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome. This happened during Felix’s pontificate.

faqs.question: Did Pope Felix I die as a martyr?
faqs.answer: The Liber Pontificalis calls him a martyr, but his pontificate fell during a time of peace for Christians, and historians think the title likely came from confusion with another Felix.

directAnswer: St. Eutychian was the twenty-seventh bishop of Rome, from 275 to 283, during a long period of peace for the Church. He is one of the most obscure popes: apart from his dates and his burial in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, almost nothing reliable is known about him.

sections.h2: A Pope of the Quiet Years
paras: Eutychian led the Roman Church during the decades between the edict of Gallienus in 260 and the outbreak of the Great Persecution under Diocletian in 303. Christian communities grew during this time, but the sources say little about individual bishops, and Eutychian is no exception. Eusebius mentions only his succession and length of office.

The Liber Pontificalis says he came from Luni in Tuscany and credits him with permitting the blessing of crops such as beans and grapes at the altar. It also claims he personally buried hundreds of martyrs, which is implausible since there was no persecution in his day.

Eutychian was the last pope buried in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, where fragments of his epitaph were discovered in the nineteenth century. Although later tradition called him a martyr, the early Roman calendar lists him among bishops rather than martyrs. His feast falls in early December.

keyFacts: Twenty-seventh bishop of Rome, January 4, 275, to December 7, 283
Reigned during the long peace before Diocletian’s persecution
Liber Pontificalis names Luni as his birthplace
Credited by later tradition with blessings of crops at the altar
Last pope buried in the papal crypt of St. Callixtus

faqs.question: Why is so little known about Pope St. Eutychian?
faqs.answer: He reigned in a peaceful period that left few records, and early historians like Eusebius mention only his dates. Most details about him come from the much later Liber Pontificalis, which is often unreliable for this era.

faqs.question: Was Pope Eutychian a martyr?
faqs.answer: Later tradition calls him one, but there was no persecution during his pontificate, and the oldest Roman records list him as a bishop, not a martyr.

directAnswer: St. Caius (also Gaius) was the twenty-eighth bishop of Rome, serving from 283 to 296, in the years before Diocletian’s Great Persecution. Little is known about him beyond his dates and his burial in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus. Later legend makes him a relative of Diocletian and a martyr, but these claims are unreliable.

paras: Caius governed the Roman Church for about thirteen years, a long pontificate for the period. Diocletian came to power in 284, but his persecution did not begin until 303, years after Caius’s death, so the Church continued to enjoy freedom and growth during his time.

The Liber Pontificalis says Caius was a Dalmatian from Salona and claims he established that a cleric must pass through each of the minor orders before becoming a bishop. A later legend makes him a relative of Diocletian, but there is no evidence for this.

Caius was buried in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, in a section near the papal crypt, where his epitaph was found in the nineteenth century. His legendary martyrdom by beheading does not fit the timeline, and early Roman records list him among bishops rather than martyrs.
His feast day is April 22, shared with Pope St. Soter.
